content.title: About
content.content: Marmalade is a sweet spread made by cooking fruit puree (most commonly orange, lemon, or berry) with sugar and sometimes a gelling agent (pectin, gelatin). It has a bright fruit flavor, aromatic scent, and a glossy texture, suitable for spreading on bread, using in baking, and as a filling for desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “marmalade” derives from the Arabic “murabbaha,” meaning “preserve.”
In the 19th century Russia, marmalade was often made from apples and pears before citrus varieties became popular.
Pectin, a natural gelling component, is found in the skins of most fruits and gives marmalade its characteristic jelly‑like consistency.
Marmalade is frequently used as a base for flavored candies and lozenges.
In some countries (e.g., the United Kingdom) the term “marmalade” refers specifically to citrus marmalade, usually made from oranges.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Citrus marmalade provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Fruit polyphenols in marmalade help neutralize free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Pectin acts as soluble fiber, promoting regular bowel movements.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The sugar in marmalade supplies rapid glucose, useful for low‑energy situations.

items.title: Enhances taste perception
items.content: The sweet‑tart balance stimulates saliva production, aiding digestion.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large servings can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to citrus components.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature may irritate the stomach lining if consumed in excess.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial marmalades may contain artificial preservatives and flavorings that some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Marmalade can be spread on toast, used as a filling for cupcakes, buns, and pancakes, stirred into yogurt, cottage cheese, or ricotta, and incorporated into sauces for meat or fish. It also adds a bright fruit note to desserts that call for a sweet‑tart element.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store marmalade in a tightly sealed jar in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 2–3 weeks. Discard if mold appears or the flavor changes.
